questions.sampleBand9: Without a doubt, my favorite subject in high school was philosophy. questions.sampleAnswer: My favourite subject was literature, and I think the reasons for that reveal something about how I engage with learning more broadly. What I loved about literature was that it was the one subject that seemed to take seriously the question of what it means to be human—the great novels and plays we studied weren't just texts to be analysed, they were explorations of experience, consciousness, and moral complexity that felt genuinely relevant to my own life. A good literature teacher can make a text feel alive in a way that changes how you see the world, and I was fortunate to have a teacher who had that ability. I was also drawn to the way literature rewarded close attention and careful thinking rather than the memorisation of facts—you could always go deeper, always find more to say, which suited my way of thinking. History was a close second—I've always been fascinated by the question of how the present came to be, and the best history teaching connects the past to the present in ways that illuminate both.

questions.sampleAnswer: With a small number of them, yes—and I think the pattern of which friendships have survived is quite revealing. The friends I've maintained contact with are those where the connection was based on genuine compatibility rather than simply proximity—we happened to be in the same class or the same social group, but we also genuinely liked each other and had things in common beyond the shared context of school. The friendships that were primarily situational—based on convenience or social necessity rather than genuine affinity—have naturally faded as the shared context disappeared. I think this is a fairly universal pattern: most people find that their circle of genuine friends from school is smaller than they might have expected, but those that remain are often among the most enduring relationships in their lives. Social media has made it easier to maintain a kind of peripheral contact with a much wider group of former classmates, which is pleasant in a low-key way, but I'd distinguish that from the deeper friendships that require actual investment of time and attention.

questions.sampleAnswer: In some ways yes, in others definitely not—and I think the honest answer requires distinguishing between what was genuinely good about that period and what I'm actually nostalgic for. I also miss the intensity of certain friendships and experiences that are particular to adolescence. What I don't miss is the anxiety and self-consciousness that are also characteristic of that period—the acute sensitivity to social judgement, the uncertainty about identity, the pressure to fit in. I think the most honest answer is that I appreciate what that period gave me without particularly wanting to return to it.

I'd like to describe an occasion from about three years ago when I accidentally broke a ceramic vase that had belonged to my grandmother—an incident that was more emotionally significant than it might sound.

The vase was a fairly large, hand-painted ceramic piece that my grandmother had brought back from a trip she made to Portugal many years before I was born. It had sat on a shelf in her home for as long as I could remember, and after she passed away, it came to me as part of a small collection of objects I kept as mementos of her. It wasn't particularly valuable in monetary terms, but it had considerable sentimental significance.

The incident happened at home, on an ordinary weekday evening. I was rearranging some items on a bookshelf—something I do periodically when I feel the urge to reorganise my space—and I moved the vase to a different position. As I was placing it down, I misjudged the distance to the edge of the shelf, and it fell. It hit the floor and shattered into several pieces. The whole thing happened in a fraction of a second, but I remember the sound of it breaking very clearly.

My immediate reaction was a combination of shock and genuine sadness—not the kind of frustration you feel when you break something replaceable, but a more specific grief at the loss of something irreplaceable. I stood there for a moment, looking at the pieces on the floor, feeling quite upset.

Afterwards, I carefully collected all the fragments and spent some time trying to piece them back together. I managed to repair most of it using a specialist ceramic adhesive, though the cracks remained visible. I actually found the Japanese concept of kintsugi—the practice of repairing broken pottery with gold, treating the breakage as part of the object's history rather than something to be hidden—quite comforting in that context. The repaired vase now sits on a different shelf, and the visible repairs feel like a part of its story rather than a disfigurement. It was a lesson in how objects can carry emotional weight, and how loss, even of something small, can be genuinely affecting.

U mening xotiramda qolganicha, uning uyidagi tokchada turardi va u vafot etganidan keyin, u menga uning xotiralari sifatida saqlagan kichik buyumlar to'plamining bir qismi sifatida keldi. U pul jihatidan unchalik qimmat bo'lmasa-da, sezilarli hissiy ahamiyatga ega edi.

Voqea uyda, oddiy ish kuni kechqurun sodir bo'ldi. Men kitob javonidagi ba'zi narsalarni qayta joylashtirayotgan edim - o'z joyimni qayta tashkil qilish istagi paydo bo'lganda, men vaqti-vaqti bilan shunday qilaman - va vazani boshqa joyga ko'chirdim. Uni qo'yayotganimda, tokchaning chetigacha bo'lgan masofani noto'g'ri baholadim va u tushib ketdi. U polga urilib, bir nechta bo'laklarga bo'linib ketdi. Hamma narsa bir lahzada sodir bo'ldi, lekin uning sinishi ovozi juda aniq esimda.

Mening birinchi reaksiyam hayrat va chinakam qayg'u aralashmasi edi - almashtirish mumkin bo'lgan narsani sindirganingizda his qiladigan umidsizlik emas, balki almashtirib bo'lmaydigan narsaning yo'qolishidan kelib chiqadigan o'ziga xos qayg'u. Men bir lahza turib, poldagi bo'laklarga qarab, juda xafa bo'ldim.

Keyin men barcha bo'laklarni ehtiyotkorlik bilan yig'ib oldim va ularni qayta tiklashga harakat qilib, biroz vaqt o'tkazdim. Men ko'p qismini maxsus seramika yopishtiruvchi yordamida tuzatishga muvaffaq bo'ldim, garchi yoriqlar ko'rinib qoldi. Men aslida kintsugi yapon tushunchasini - singan kulolchilikni oltin bilan ta'mirlash, sinishni yashirishdan ko'ra ob'ekt tarixining bir qismi sifatida qabul qilish amaliyotini - shu nuqtai nazardan juda taskin beruvchi deb topdim. Ta'mirlangan vaza hozir boshqa tokchada turibdi va ko'rinadigan ta'mirlashlar uni xunuklashtirishdan ko'ra uning hikoyasining bir qismi kabi tuyuladi. Bu narsalar hissiy yukni qanday olib yurishi va yo'qotish, hatto kichik narsa bo'lsa ham, chinakam ta'sir qilishi mumkinligi haqida saboq edi.

For certain types of clothing—particularly technical sportswear, workwear, or garments requiring precise construction—factory production may actually produce a superior result. However, for most clothing, and particularly for tailored or bespoke garments, handmade production allows for a level of personalisation, attention to detail, and quality of materials that factory production cannot match. The economics of factory production create pressure to use cheaper materials, faster processes, and lower labour costs, all of which tend to compromise quality. The fast fashion industry in particular has driven quality dramatically downward—garments that are designed to be worn a few times and discarded are a far cry from the durable, well-constructed clothing that was the norm a few generations ago. questions.sampleAnswer: The things most commonly broken at home tend to fall into a few predictable categories, and the pattern reveals something interesting about how we use our domestic spaces. Fragile items—glassware, ceramics, and crockery—are among the most frequently broken, simply because they're used daily and are inherently vulnerable to the kind of accidental contact and dropping that is inevitable in a busy household. Electronic devices—phones, tablets, and laptops—are also extremely commonly broken, particularly their screens, which are both fragile and constantly handled. Furniture and fittings—chairs, hinges, door handles—tend to break through gradual wear and tear rather than sudden accidents. Kitchen appliances are another common category—the combination of heat, moisture, and frequent use creates conditions that accelerate wear. Children and pets are significant factors in what gets broken at home—both introduce an element of unpredictability and energy that increases the likelihood of accidents. I think the items that are most often broken are those that combine frequent use with fragility—the more something is handled, the more opportunities there are for accidents, and the more fragile it is, the more likely any accident is to result in damage.

Oshxona jihozlari yana bir keng tarqalgan toifa - issiqlik, namlik va tez-tez ishlatishning kombinatsiyasi eskirishni tezlashtiradigan sharoitlarni yaratadi. Bolalar va uy hayvonlari uyda nima sindirilishida muhim omil hisoblanadi - ikkalasi ham baxtsiz hodisalar ehtimolini oshiradigan kutilmaganlik va energiyani olib kiradi. Menimcha, eng ko'p sindiriladigan narsalar tez-tez ishlatilishi va mo'rtligi uyg'unlashgan narsalardir - narsa qanchalik ko'p ishlatilsa, baxtsiz hodisalar uchun shunchalik ko'p imkoniyat bo'ladi va u qanchalik mo'rt bo'lsa, har qanday baxtsiz hodisa shikastlanishga olib kelishi ehtimoli shunchalik yuqori bo'ladi.

questions.prompt: Do you think elderly people should teach young people to fix things?

vocabulary.title: Q16 - Elderly Teaching Young to Fix Things
sentenceStarters: Yes, I think this is genuinely valuable...
Beyond the practical dimension, intergenerational...
There's also a broader cultural argument...

questions.sampleBand5: Well, um, I think older people can, you know, show young people how to, like, fix things. It's, um, good for them. They know more about it, maybe? I think so.
questions.sampleBand6: Yes, I think it's a good idea. Actually, elderly people have a lot of experience. They grew up in a time when things were fixed more often than replaced. So, they could teach valuable skills. Sometimes, it's hard to learn these things from books.
questions.sampleBand7: I definitely think there's value in that. Elderly people often possess practical skills that younger generations might lack. They've picked up knowledge through years of experience, and passing that on could be incredibly beneficial. It's also a good way to bridge the generation gap, I believe.
questions.sampleBand8: Yes, I think that’s a fantastic idea. Essentially, it's about passing down valuable skills. Older generations often have a wealth of practical knowledge that’s becoming increasingly rare. They can teach young people not just how to fix things, but also the importance of resourcefulness and sustainability. Plus, it creates a meaningful connection between generations, which is a win-win, really.
questions.sampleBand9: Absolutely, I believe that encouraging intergenerational skill-sharing, particularly in areas like practical repairs, is incredibly valuable. Older individuals often possess a treasure trove of hands-on knowledge accumulated over a lifetime, which is something you simply can’t pick up from a manual or online tutorial. Not only does it empower younger people with essential life skills and boost their confidence, but it also allows the elderly to feel valued and contribute to society in a meaningful way. It’s a case of two birds with one stone, really.
questions.sampleAnswer: Yes, I think this is genuinely valuable, and the argument for it operates on several levels simultaneously. At the most practical level, the repair skills that older generations possess—fixing appliances, mending clothes, maintaining tools, basic carpentry and plumbing—are genuinely useful and are becoming increasingly rare among younger people. The transmission of these skills from older to younger generations would reduce waste, save money, and increase self-reliance. Beyond the practical dimension, intergenerational skill-sharing has social and relational benefits that are equally important. The process of teaching and learning creates opportunities for meaningful connection between generations that might not otherwise interact—it gives older people a sense of purpose and contribution, and gives younger people access to accumulated wisdom and experience. There's also a broader cultural argument: a society that values and transmits practical skills is one that maintains a connection to the material world and to the knowledge of how things work, which I think is important for both individual wellbeing and collective resilience. Initiatives like repair cafés, where people of different ages come together to fix things, are a promising model for how this kind of intergenerational knowledge transfer can be facilitated in a modern context.
questions.uzSampleBand5: Xo'sh, e-e, menimcha, keksa odamlar yoshlarga narsalarni qanday tuzatishni ko'rsatishi mumkin, bilasizmi. Bu, e-e, ular uchun yaxshi. Ular bu haqda ko'proq bilishadi, balki? Men shunday deb o'ylayman.
questions.uzSampleBand6: Ha, menimcha, bu yaxshi fikr. Aslida, keksa odamlarning tajribasi ko'p. Ular narsalar almashtirilgandan ko'ra ko'proq tuzatiladigan davrda o'sgan. Shunday qilib, ular qimmatli ko'nikmalarni o'rgatishi mumkin. Ba'zan, bu narsalarni kitoblardan o'rganish qiyin.
questions.uzSampleBand7: Men aniq bu narsaning qimmati bor deb o'ylayman. Keksa odamlarda ko'pincha yosh avlodlarda bo'lmasligi mumkin bo'lgan amaliy ko'nikmalar mavjud. Ular yillar davomida tajriba orttirib olishgan va buni o'rgatish juda foydali bo'lishi mumkin. Shuningdek, bu avlodlar o'rtasidagi tafovutni bartaraf etishning yaxshi usuli, deb o'ylayman.
questions.uzSampleBand8: Ha, menimcha, bu ajoyib fikr. Aslida, bu qimmatli ko'nikmalarni o'tkazish haqida. Keksa avlodlarda ko'pincha tobora kamayib borayotgan amaliy bilimlar mavjud. Ular yoshlarga nafaqat narsalarni qanday tuzatishni, balki tejamkorlik va barqarorlikning ahamiyatini ham o'rgatishi mumkin. Bundan tashqari, bu avlodlar o'rtasida mazmunli aloqa yaratadi, bu haqiqatan ham yutuqli.
questions.uzSampleBand9: Albatta, menimcha, avlodlararo ko'nikmalarni almashishni, ayniqsa amaliy ta'mirlash kabi sohalarda rag'batlantirish juda qimmatli. Keksa odamlarda bir umr davomida to'plangan qo'l bilan qilingan bilimlar xazinasi mavjud, buni shunchaki qo'llanma yoki onlayn darslikdan o'rgana olmaysiz. Bu nafaqat yoshlarni muhim hayotiy ko'nikmalar bilan kuchaytiradi va ularning ishonchini oshiradi, balki keksalarga o'zini qadrlash va jamiyatga mazmunli hissa qo'shish imkoniyatini beradi. Bu, aslida, bir tosh bilan ikki quyonni urish.
questions.uzSampleAnswer: Ha, menimcha, bu haqiqatan ham qimmatli va buning foydasi bir nechta darajalarda bir vaqtning o'zida namoyon bo'ladi. Eng amaliy darajada, keksa avlodlarning ta'mirlash ko'nikmalari - jihozlarni tuzatish, kiyimlarni yamash, asboblarni saqlash, oddiy duradgorlik va santexnika - haqiqatan ham foydali va yoshlar orasida tobora kamayib bormoqda. Ushbu ko'nikmalarni kattalardan kichiklarga o'tkazish chiqindilarni kamaytiradi, pulni tejaydi va o'ziga ishonchni oshiradi. Amaliy o'lchamdan tashqari, avlodlararo ko'nikmalarni almashish ijtimoiy va munosabatlarga oid foydalarga ega, ular ham muhim. O'qitish va o'rganish jarayoni turli avlodlar o'rtasida mazmunli aloqa uchun imkoniyatlar yaratadi, aks holda ular o'zaro aloqada bo'lmasligi mumkin - bu keksalarga maqsad va hissa qo'shish tuyg'usini beradi, yoshlarga esa to'plangan donolik va tajribaga ega bo'lish imkoniyatini beradi. Bundan tashqari, kengroq madaniy bahs ham bor: amaliy ko'nikmalarni qadrlaydigan va o'rgatadigan jamiyat moddiy dunyo bilan va narsalar qanday ishlashini bilish bilan aloqani saqlaydi, bu, menimcha, ham individual farovonlik, ham jamoaviy chidamlilik uchun muhimdir. Turli yoshdagi odamlar narsalarni tuzatish uchun birga yig'iladigan ta'mirlash kafesi kabi tashabbuslar zamonaviy sharoitda avlodlararo bilim almashishni qanday osonlashtirish mumkinligining istiqbolli modelidir.

questions.prompt: Why do some people prefer to buy new things rather than repair old ones?

vocabulary.title: Q17 - Buying New vs Repairing Old
idioms: out with the old in with the new
if it ain't broke don't fix it
sentenceStarters: The preference for replacement over repair...
Psychologically, there's the appeal of novelty...
I think reversing this trend requires...

questions.sampleBand5: Well, um, I think some people, throw away old things because it's easier. It's, like, less trouble. And, um, new things are, you know, new. So yeah. It's simple.
questions.sampleBand6: I think there are a few reasons. Um, sometimes it's just simply more convenient to buy something new. Repairing things can be a real hassle, finding someone to do it, the cost of parts... And also, people like having the latest models, you know? So, yeah, convenience and wanting something new, I guess.
questions.sampleBand7: Well, I think a major factor is probably convenience. It can be a time-consuming process to find someone to repair something, and frankly, sometimes the repair costs can be almost as much as buying a new item. Plus, there's the allure of having something shiny and new with all the latest features. People are often tempted by that, I think.
questions.sampleBand8: I suppose there are several contributing factors. Firstly, we live in a society that values convenience above all else. Repairing something often requires effort, time, and sometimes specialized skills. Secondly, the perceived cost can be a deterrent. People often assume that repairs will be expensive, and it’s sometimes cheaper to just fork out for a new one. Finally, there's the psychological aspect. New products are often associated with status and progress.
questions.sampleBand9: I believe a confluence of factors is at play here. One significant aspect is the prevailing culture of consumerism, where planned obsolescence is almost built into products. It’s often deliberately made difficult or expensive to repair things, pushing consumers towards repurchase. Moreover, the constant barrage of advertising and marketing campaigns creates a desire for the latest models and technologies, playing on our sense of status and belonging. To top it off, many lack the necessary skills or time to undertake repairs themselves, making buying new the seemingly easier option.
questions.sampleAnswer: The preference for replacement over repair is driven by a combination of economic, psychological, and cultural factors that are deeply embedded in modern consumer society. Economically, the calculation has shifted dramatically in recent decades—in many product categories, the cost of repair now exceeds the cost of replacement, particularly for electronics and cheap consumer goods. This is partly a result of deliberate design choices by manufacturers—products are increasingly designed to be difficult or impossible to repair, a practice known as planned obsolescence, which ensures a steady stream of replacement purchases. Psychologically, there's the appeal of novelty—a new product is exciting in a way that a repaired old one isn't, and consumer culture has been very effective at associating newness with desirability and progress. There's also the convenience factor—taking something to be repaired requires time, effort, and uncertainty about the outcome, while buying something new is immediate and predictable. Culturally, repair has lost much of the social status it once had—in previous generations, being able to fix things was a valued skill; today, it's often seen as a sign of not being able to afford something new. I think reversing this trend requires both economic incentives—making repair cheaper and replacement more expensive through taxation and regulation—and cultural change that revalues repair as a skill and a practice.
questions.uzSampleBand5: Xo'sh, menimcha, ba'zi odamlar eski narsalarni tashlab yuborishadi, chunki bu osonroq. Bu, bilasizmi, kamroq tashvish. Va, yangi narsalar yangi, bilasizmi. Xullas, shunaqa. Oddiy.
questions.uzSampleBand6: Menimcha, buning bir nechta sabablari bor. Ba'zan shunchaki yangi narsa sotib olish shunchaki qulayroq. Narsalarni ta'mirlash juda qiyin bo'lishi mumkin, buni qiladigan odamni topish, ehtiyot qismlarning narxi... Va odamlar eng so'nggi modellarga ega bo'lishni xohlashadi, bilasizmi? Xullas, ha, qulaylik va yangi narsani xohlash, menimcha.
questions.uzSampleBand7: Xo'sh, menimcha, asosiy omil, ehtimol, qulaylikdir. Biror narsani ta'mirlash uchun odamni topish vaqt talab qiladigan jarayon bo'lishi mumkin va ochig'ini aytsam, ba'zan ta'mirlash narxi yangi buyumni sotib olish bilan deyarli bir xil bo'lishi mumkin. Bundan tashqari, barcha so'nggi funksiyalarga ega bo'lgan yorqin va yangi narsaga ega bo'lish jozibasi bor. Odamlar ko'pincha bunga vasvasaga tushishadi, menimcha.
questions.uzSampleBand8: O'ylashimcha, bir nechta omillar bor. Birinchidan, biz qulaylikni hamma narsadan ustun qo'yadigan jamiyatda yashaymiz. Biror narsani ta'mirlash ko'pincha harakat, vaqt va ba'zan maxsus ko'nikmalarni talab qiladi. Ikkinchidan, taxminiy narx to'siq bo'lishi mumkin. Odamlar ko'pincha ta'mirlash qimmatga tushadi deb o'ylashadi va ba'zan yangisini to'lash osonroq. Nihoyat, psixologik jihat ham bor. Yangi mahsulotlar ko'pincha maqom va taraqqiyot bilan bog'liq.
questions.uzSampleBand9: Ishonamanki, bu yerda bir nechta omillar o'zaro ta'sir qilmoqda. Muhim jihatlardan biri bu iste'molchilikning hukmron madaniyatidir, bu yerda rejalashtirilgan eskirish mahsulotlarga deyarli o'rnatilgan. Narsalarni ta'mirlash ko'pincha ataylab qiyin yoki qimmat qilinadi, bu iste'molchilarni qayta sotib olishga undaydi. Bundan tashqari, doimiy reklama va marketing kampaniyalari so'nggi modellar va texnologiyalarga bo'lgan istakni yaratadi, bu bizning maqom va mansublik hissimizga ta'sir qiladi. Buning ustiga, ko'pchilikda ta'mirlashni mustaqil ravishda amalga oshirish uchun zarur ko'nikmalar yoki vaqt yo'q, bu esa yangisini sotib olishni osonroq variantga aylantiradi.
questions.uzSampleAnswer: Eski narsalarni ta'mirlashdan ko'ra yangisini sotib olish afzalligi zamonaviy iste'mol jamiyatiga chuqur singib ketgan iqtisodiy, psixologik va madaniy omillar kombinatsiyasi bilan bog'liq. Iqtisodiy jihatdan, so'nggi o'n yilliklarda hisob-kitob keskin o'zgardi — ko'plab mahsulot toifalarida ta'mirlash narxi hozirda almashtirish narxidan oshib ketadi, ayniqsa elektronika va arzon iste'mol tovarlari uchun. Bu qisman ishlab chiqaruvchilarning ataylab dizayn tanlovi natijasidir — mahsulotlar tobora ta'mirlash qiyin yoki imkonsiz bo'lishi uchun mo'ljallangan, bu rejalashtirilgan eskirish amaliyoti bo'lib, bu almashtirish xaridlari oqimini ta'minlaydi. Psixologik jihatdan, yangilikning jozibasi bor — yangi mahsulot ta'mirlangan eski mahsulotga o'xshamaydi va iste'mol madaniyati yangilikni maqbullik va taraqqiyot bilan bog'lashda juda samarali bo'ldi. Bundan tashqari, qulaylik omili ham bor — biror narsani ta'mirlash uchun olib borish vaqt, kuch va natija haqida noaniqlikni talab qiladi, yangi narsa sotib olish esa tez va bashorat qilinadi. Madaniy jihatdan ta'mirlash o'z vaqtida ega bo'lgan ijtimoiy maqomining ko'p qismini yo'qotdi — avvalgi avlodlarda narsalarni tuzata olish qimmatli mahorat edi; bugungi kunda bu ko'pincha yangi narsani sotib olishga qurbi yetmasligining belgisi sifatida ko'riladi. Menimcha, bu tendentsiyani o'zgartirish iqtisodiy rag'batlantirishlarni ham (ta'mirlashni arzonlashtirish va soliq solish va tartibga solish orqali almashtirishni qimmatlashtirish) va ta'mirlashni mahorat va amaliyot sifatida qayta baholaydigan madaniy o'zgarishlarni talab qiladi.
